intro: Sirens on a spring night. A field so flat you can see the next town's water tower. A shadow that shrinks and swings across the blacktop. A river that flows the wrong way. Every one of those is a clue. This unit is about Earth: its weather, its ground, its place in space, and the people living on it.

You will measure weather with real tools. You will find the pattern hiding in a year of numbers. You will read a cliff like a book, oldest page on the bottom. You will find out why Illinois is flat and why the sun seems to move. You will learn why summer is not about being closer to the sun. And you will see where all of Earth's water really is.

By the end, you can explain a tornado warning and a pothole. You can explain a shadow stick, a full moon and a backward river. And you can argue with evidence about a hard question. When people change Earth's systems, what happens next? Who has to live with it?
bigQuestion: What patterns shape Earth's weather, land and sky, and how do people fit into those systems?

title: Earth, Weather and Space

chapters.title: Weather and Climate
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we measure weather, find its patterns, and stay safe when it turns dangerous?

story.title: The Night the Sirens Went Off
story.kicker: A warm spring evening in Illinois turns strange, and then the whole town hears the same sound.
paragraphs: It was the first hot evening of May. Maya sat on the porch doing homework. The air felt thick and sticky. Her grandfather looked west and frowned. The sky over the cornfields had turned a strange green-gray. The wind, which had blown all day, suddenly stopped.

Inside, the TV showed a map of Illinois. A red box covered their county. A voice said the words 'tornado warning.' That meant a tornado had been seen, or radar had spotted one forming. A watch means conditions are right. A warning means it is happening now.

Then the sirens began. A long, rising howl came from the pole by the fire station. Maya's grandfather did not run. He walked. He turned off the stove, grabbed the flashlight, and led everyone to the basement. They sat under the stairs, away from the windows, with the weather radio on.

Hail hit the house like handfuls of gravel. The wind roared. Maya counted her breaths. Then, just as fast, it was quiet. Rain fell soft and steady. The radio said the tornado had touched down four miles north, in an empty field, and lifted again.

The next morning, the sky was clean and blue. A neighbor's trampoline sat in a tree. Maya wanted to know everything. Why did the sky turn green? How did the radar see the storm? Why do tornadoes love Illinois in spring? This chapter is her list of questions, with answers.
story.think: Maya's grandfather walked to the basement instead of running outside to look. Why was that the smart choice?

lessons.title: What Weather Is
lessons.mainIdea: Weather is what the air is doing right now, and we measure it with tools instead of guessing.
reading: Step outside. Is the air hot or cold? Wet or dry? Still or windy? All of that is *weather*. Weather is the condition of the air at one place and one time. It can change in an hour. A sunny morning can become a stormy afternoon.

Scientists do not trust the word 'hot.' Hot to one person is warm to another. So they measure. A *thermometer* measures *temperature*, how warm the air is. In the United States we use degrees Fahrenheit. Water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F at sea level.

A measurement is a number anyone can check. If you write 68 °F in a notebook every day at noon, you have data. After a month, you can see a pattern. That is the first job of a weather scientist: measure, write it down, and look for the pattern.

words.d: what the air is doing at one place and time: its temperature, wind, clouds and rain
a tool that measures how warm or cold something is
a measure of how hot or cold the air is, given in degrees

look.title: Two Thermometers
look.text: A class hangs one thermometer in the sun on the brick wall. They hang another in the shade under a tree. At noon the sunny one reads 91 °F. The shady one reads 78 °F. The air is the same air. Weather stations always put thermometers in a shaded white box with slits for air.
look.prompt: Which thermometer tells the true air temperature, and why does the other one read so high?

check.q: Which of these is a weather measurement, not a guess?
choices: The sky looks kind of gray.
check.why: A number from a tool can be checked by anyone. The others are feelings or guesses.

check.q: What does a thermometer measure?
check.why: A thermometer measures temperature, how hot or cold the air is.

check.q: Why do scientists write down the temperature every day instead of once?
choices: One number cannot show a pattern
check.why: Patterns only show up when you collect many measurements over time.

lessons.title: Rain, Snow and the Gauge
lessons.mainIdea: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds, and a rain gauge measures how much.
reading: Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all *precipitation*. That long word just means water falling out of the sky. Rain is liquid drops. Snow is ice crystals. Hail is balls of ice built up inside a tall storm cloud. Sleet is rain that froze on the way down.

To measure rain, you need a *rain gauge*. It is a straight-sided tube with marks on it. Rain falls in, and you read the depth. If the tube shows 1 inch, then 1 inch of rain fell on every part of the yard. A bucket would not work well because its sides slope.

Snow is trickier. Ten inches of fluffy snow may melt down to only 1 inch of water. So weather stations measure snow two ways. They measure how deep it is with a ruler. Then they melt it and measure the water. Chicago gets roughly 38 inches of precipitation in a normal year.

words.d: water that falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail
a marked tube that catches rain so you can measure how deep it is

look.title: The Leaning Bucket
look.text: Two students measure a storm. One uses a straight glass tube. The other uses a plastic bucket that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. After the rain, the tube shows 1 inch. The bucket shows 2 inches. They argue about who is right. The storm dropped the same rain on both.
look.prompt: Why does the bucket read higher than the tube, and which one should the class trust?

check.q: Which of these is NOT a kind of precipitation?
check.why: Fog is a cloud near the ground. Water in fog does not fall. Snow, hail and sleet all fall from clouds.

check.q: Why does a rain gauge need straight sides?
choices: So the depth means the same everywhere
So it looks nice on a table
check.why: With straight sides, 1 inch in the tube equals 1 inch of rain on the whole yard.

check.q: Ten inches of snow melted into about 1 inch of water. What does that tell you?
choices: Snow is mostly air between ice crystals
Snow turns into less water than it holds
check.why: Fluffy snow has lots of air in it, so it melts down to much less water.

lessons.title: Where the Wind Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: Wind is moving air, and we measure both its direction and its speed.
reading: Air is real stuff, even though you cannot see it. When air moves, we call it *wind*. Wind starts because the sun heats some places more than others. Warm air rises. Cooler air slides in to take its place. That slide is the wind you feel on your face.

A *wind vane* shows direction. Its arrow points into the wind. A north wind blows from the north toward the south. Wind is always named for where it comes from. An *anemometer* measures speed. Its little cups spin faster when the wind blows harder.

Wind direction is a clue. In Illinois, a south wind in spring often brings warm, wet air from the Gulf of Mexico. A north wind in winter brings cold air from Canada. Watch which way the flag on your school points. It is telling you something about tomorrow.

words.d: air that is moving from one place to another
a tool with an arrow that points into the wind to show its direction
a tool with spinning cups that measures how fast the wind blows

look.title: The Flag and the Smoke
look.text: At 8 a.m. the school flag points south, so the wind is from the north. The air is 40 °F. By 3 p.m. the flag has swung around and points north. Now the wind is from the south. The air has warmed to 62 °F. Smoke from a chimney across the street leans the same way as the flag.
look.prompt: What changed during the day, and what do you predict the temperature will do tomorrow if the south wind keeps blowing?

check.q: A 'west wind' is blowing. Which way is the air moving?
choices: From the west toward the east
check.why: Winds are named for where they come from. A west wind comes from the west.

check.q: What makes air begin to move as wind?
choices: The sun heating some places more than others
check.why: Uneven heating makes warm air rise and cooler air slide in, which is wind.

check.q: Which tool would you use to find out how fast the wind is blowing?
check.why: An anemometer's spinning cups measure wind speed. A wind vane only shows direction.

lessons.title: Seasons in the Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Weather data collected over a year shows a repeating pattern called the seasons.
reading: One day of weather is just one day. But a year of numbers tells a story. Look at Chicago's average high temperature month by month. It climbs from winter to summer and falls again. That rise and fall is the pattern of the *seasons*.

An *average* is a way to squeeze many numbers into one. Add up thirty daily highs for January. Divide by thirty. That is January's average high. The average hides the wild days. It shows the usual day instead.

Patterns let you predict. If January in Chicago averages about 32 °F, you can expect ice next January too. You cannot say which day will snow. But you can say winter coats will be needed. That is the difference between a single day and a pattern.

words.d: the repeating pattern of warm and cold parts of the year: spring, summer, fall and winter
one number that stands for a whole group of numbers, found by adding them and dividing

look.title: Chicago's Average High Temperature
look.cite: NOAA climate normals for Chicago, rounded
look.prompt: Which two months have almost the same average high, and why might that be even though they are in different seasons?

check.q: Why do scientists use an average instead of listing every day?
choices: One number shows the usual day
Averages take less time to measure
check.why: An average squeezes many days into one number that shows what is typical.

check.q: Chicago's average July high is about 84 °F. What can you safely predict?
choices: Every July day will be exactly 84 °F
Next July will have no rain
Next July will be warm in general
check.why: A pattern predicts the usual weather, not any single day.

check.q: The average high rises from January to July. What causes that pattern?
choices: The seasons changing through the year
More people living in the city in summer
check.why: The rise and fall of temperature through the year is the pattern of the seasons.

lessons.title: Climate Is the Long Story
lessons.mainIdea: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years; weather is what happens today.
reading: Here is a saying that helps. Weather is your mood. *Climate* is your personality. Weather is what the air does today. Climate is what the air usually does, measured over thirty years or more. A cold day in July does not change Chicago's climate.

Scientists describe a climate with long-term averages. What is the usual January? The usual July? How much rain falls in a normal year? Illinois has cold winters, hot summers and rain in every season. A desert climate has very little rain at all.

Climate matters because living things and people plan around it. Farmers in Illinois plant corn in spring because the pattern says frost is over. Roofs here are built to hold snow. If a place's climate slowly shifts, those plans have to shift too. Scientists track this with careful records.

words.d: the usual weather of a place, found by averaging many years of measurements
over many years, not just days or months

look.title: One Warm Day in January
look.text: On January 12, the temperature in Springfield reaches 61 °F. Kids wear shorts. A student says, 'Illinois has a warm climate now.' Her teacher pulls up thirty years of records. January's average high is still around 35 °F. The next week, it is 14 °F and snowing.
look.prompt: Was the student describing weather or climate? What would she need to see in the records to say the climate had changed?

check.q: Which sentence is about climate, not weather?
choices: Phoenix is dry almost every year.
check.why: Climate is the usual pattern over many years. The others describe one day.

check.q: About how long a record do scientists use to describe a climate?
check.why: Climate is based on long-term averages, usually thirty years or more.

check.q: Why do Illinois farmers plant corn in spring rather than in February?
choices: The climate pattern says frost is usually over
Corn seeds are only sold in spring
The soil is frozen all summer
check.why: Farmers plan around the climate, the usual pattern of when frost ends.

lessons.title: Climates Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Different places on Earth have very different climates because of sunlight, oceans, mountains and lakes.
reading: Why is it snowing in Chicago while it is hot in Miami? Part of the answer is sunlight. Places near the *equator* get strong, direct sun all year. Places near the poles get weak, slanted sun. In between, like Illinois, the sun's strength changes with the seasons.

Oceans and big lakes matter too. Water heats up and cools down slowly. A city by the sea has milder winters and cooler summers than a city far inland. Chicago's lakefront is cooler on a hot day than a suburb 30 miles west. That is Lake Michigan at work.

Mountains block wet air. Rain falls on one side. The other side stays dry, a *rain shadow*. Seattle gets rain most of the year. Phoenix, in the desert, gets very little. Look at the numbers and you will see how different climates can be.

words.d: the imaginary line around the middle of Earth where the sun is strongest
the dry side of a mountain range, where the wet air has already dropped its rain

look.title: Rain and Snow in a Normal Year
look.prompt: Chicago and Seattle get about the same amount, but Seattle is famous for rain. What could be different about how it falls?

check.q: Why are places near the equator warm all year?
choices: They get strong, direct sunlight all year
They are closer to the sun
check.why: Direct sunlight near the equator is stronger than the slanted light near the poles.

check.q: Why is the Chicago lakefront cooler than a town 30 miles inland on a hot summer day?
choices: Water heats up more slowly than land
check.why: Water changes temperature slowly, so a big lake keeps the nearby air milder.

check.q: A town sits on the far side of a mountain range from the ocean. What climate would you predict?
check.why: The wet air drops its rain on the ocean side, leaving a dry rain shadow behind the mountains.

lessons.title: Tornado Watch, Tornado Warning
lessons.mainIdea: A tornado is a spinning column of air from a storm cloud, and Illinois gets dozens of them each year.
reading: A *tornado* is a spinning tube of air that reaches from a thunderstorm down to the ground. Most last only minutes. But the wind inside can be faster than any car. Illinois sits where warm, wet air from the Gulf meets cold, dry air from the north. That clash builds the storms.

Illinois gets roughly 50 tornadoes in a typical year, most in spring and early summer. The worst in history was the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925. It ran across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. It killed about 695 people, the most of any single tornado in the United States.

Scientists rate tornadoes by their damage, using the Enhanced Fujita scale, from EF0 to EF5. A *watch* means the ingredients for a tornado are present. Stay alert. A *warning* means one has been spotted or seen on radar. Go to your safe place right away.

words.d: a violently spinning column of air that reaches from a thunderstorm to the ground
a notice that conditions are right for dangerous weather; be ready
a notice that dangerous weather is happening now; take shelter

look.title: The Enhanced Fujita Scale
look.unit: mph, lowest wind speed for each rating
look.prompt: Highway cars go about 70 mph. Which tornado ratings have winds faster than a car on the highway?

check.q: A tornado warning has been issued for your county. What should you do?
choices: Go to a basement or inside room away from windows
Go outside to watch for it
Wait to see if it gets worse
check.why: A warning means a tornado is happening. Get low and away from windows right away.

check.q: Why does Illinois get so many tornadoes?
choices: It is flat, so wind spins easily
It is close to the ocean
Warm wet air and cold dry air meet there
check.why: The clash of warm Gulf air and cold northern air builds strong storms over Illinois.

check.q: What is the difference between a watch and a warning?
choices: A watch is for rain; a warning is for snow
A watch is more dangerous than a warning
A watch means be ready; a warning means it is happening
check.why: A watch says conditions are right. A warning says a tornado has been spotted or seen on radar.

lessons.title: Floods and Blizzards
lessons.mainIdea: Too much water or snow at once can be as dangerous as a tornado, and both have simple safety rules.
reading: A *flood* happens when water covers land that is usually dry. Rivers spill over after days of rain. Streets fill when storm drains cannot keep up. Moving floodwater is the danger. Just 6 inches of fast water can knock an adult down. About 12 inches can float a car.

That is why the National Weather Service has a rule for drivers. If a road is covered, turn around. You cannot see how deep the water is. You cannot see if the road is still there underneath. Most flood deaths in the United States happen in vehicles.

A *blizzard* is not just heavy snow. It is snow with strong wind, at least 35 mph, that cuts what you can see to a quarter mile or less for three hours. Chicago's great blizzard of January 1967 dropped about 23 inches. Cars and buses were buried on the roads.

words.d: when water covers land that is normally dry
a snowstorm with strong wind that makes it hard to see for hours

look.title: The Weather Service's Flood Rule
look.text: The National Weather Service warns that most flood deaths happen when people drive or walk into floodwater. It says to turn around and find another way, because you cannot tell how deep the water is or whether the road beneath it has washed out.
look.cite: National Weather Service flood safety guidance
look.prompt: Why is water on a road more dangerous than the same water in a field?

check.q: About how much fast-moving water can float a car?
check.why: Around 12 inches of moving water is enough to lift and carry most cars.

check.q: What makes a snowstorm a blizzard?
choices: Strong wind that cuts visibility for hours
check.why: A blizzard is defined by wind and poor visibility, not by how much snow falls.

check.q: A road ahead is covered with water. The safest choice is to
choices: turn around and find another route
wait in the car for it to drop
check.why: You cannot see how deep the water is or if the road is still there, so turn around.

lessons.title: Building to Stay Safe
lessons.mainIdea: People cannot stop severe weather, but good design and planning can reduce the harm it causes.
reading: Nobody can stop a tornado. But people can design for one. Storm shelters are small rooms with thick walls and heavy doors. Schools in tornado country practice drills so everyone knows the way to the inside hallway. Sirens and phone alerts give minutes of *warning* time.

Floods are fought with design too. Levees are long walls of earth along rivers. Chicago built huge tunnels deep underground, called the Deep Tunnel, to hold storm water until treatment plants can catch up. Homes in flood zones are sometimes lifted up on tall posts.

Every design has a cost and a trade-off. A levee protects one town but may push more water to the next. A shelter costs money. Engineers ask: what is the danger, how likely is it, and what is the best fix we can afford? That is engineering with weather in mind.

words.d: a strong room or building that protects people from a storm
a long wall of earth or concrete built along a river to hold back floodwater
something you give up to get something else

look.title: Design a Bus Stop
look.text: A town wants a new bus stop on a flat, open road. Summers bring thunderstorms and hail. Winters bring wind and blowing snow. The budget is small. One plan is a simple roof on posts. Another is a glass box with a door. A third is a concrete room with a heavy door, which costs five times as much.
look.prompt: Which plan would you pick, and what danger does it protect against? What does it fail to protect against?

check.q: What is the main purpose of a tornado drill at school?
choices: So everyone knows the safe route before a real storm
check.why: Practicing ahead of time means people move quickly and calmly when a warning comes.

check.q: What does a levee do?
choices: Holds back river water from a town
check.why: A levee is a long wall along a river that keeps floodwater off the land behind it.

check.q: Why do engineers talk about trade-offs when designing for weather?
choices: Because every fix has costs and limits
check.why: A shelter costs money and a levee may push water elsewhere. Every design gives up something.

lessons.title: Reading the Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Long before radar, people forecast weather by watching clouds, wind and the direction storms travel.
reading: In 1743, Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia wanted to see an eclipse. A storm blocked it. Later he learned the storm had hit Boston hours after it hit him, even though the wind had blown from the northeast. He figured out that storms travel as a whole, from one place to the next.

In 1803, an English chemist named Luke Howard gave clouds their names. *Cumulus* means heap: the puffy white ones. *Stratus* means layer: the flat gray sheet. *Cirrus* means curl: the thin high wisps. Those names are still used by every weather scientist today.

Clouds are clues. Tall, dark cumulus towers mean a thunderstorm is building. Thin cirrus often arrives a day before a rain system. A ring around the moon comes from ice crystals high up, and rain often follows. Watching the sky is real science when you write down what happens next.

words.d: puffy, heaped white clouds with flat bottoms
flat gray clouds that spread across the sky like a sheet
thin, wispy clouds very high in the sky, made of ice crystals

look.title: Franklin's Traveling Storm
look.text: Franklin wrote to a friend that a northeast storm had kept him from seeing an eclipse in Philadelphia, yet people in Boston saw it clearly and their storm came hours later. He reasoned that the storm itself was moving up the coast from the southwest, against the direction of its own wind.
look.cite: Benjamin Franklin, letter describing the storm of 1743
look.prompt: What evidence did Franklin use, and what did he conclude that people before him had missed?

check.q: What did Franklin figure out about storms?
choices: They travel as a whole from place to place
They stand still over one city
check.why: By comparing the storm's timing in two cities, Franklin saw that the storm itself had moved.

check.q: Which cloud name means 'heap' and describes puffy white clouds?
check.why: Cumulus comes from a Latin word for heap; they are the puffy piled-up clouds.

check.q: You see thin, wispy cirrus clouds high in a blue sky. What is a reasonable prediction?
choices: A tornado will hit within the hour
Rain may arrive in a day or so
It will stay clear for a month
check.why: Cirrus clouds often run ahead of a rain system by about a day.

lessons.title: Tools That See Far
lessons.mainIdea: Modern forecasts combine radar, satellites, weather balloons and computers to predict days ahead.
reading: Today's forecasters have eyes everywhere. Weather *radar* sends out radio waves. Rain, snow and hail bounce them back. The radar draws a map of where precipitation is and which way it is moving. Doppler radar can even see wind spinning inside a storm, the start of a tornado.

*Satellites* circle Earth high above the clouds. They send pictures of storms across whole oceans. Twice a day, weather stations across the country release balloons that carry tiny instruments miles into the sky. They report temperature, wind and moisture all the way up.

All of that data flows into computers that solve the equations of moving air. The result is a *forecast*, a prediction of tomorrow's weather. Forecasts a day ahead are usually right. A week ahead, they are less sure. Forecasters say 'a 40 percent chance of rain' because the air does not always do what the model says.

words.d: a tool that sends out radio waves and reads what bounces back to map rain, snow and wind
a machine in orbit around Earth that can take pictures of clouds and storms from above
a prediction of the weather to come, based on measurements and computer models

look.title: The 40 Percent Question
look.text: The forecast says 40 percent chance of rain. A student plans a picnic anyway. It rains. He says the forecast was wrong. His sister says it was right. On days like that, it rains about 4 times out of 10. It stays dry 6 times out of 10.
look.prompt: Who is right about the forecast, and how could you test whether a forecaster's percentages are honest over a whole year?

check.q: How does weather radar find rain?
choices: It bounces radio waves off falling rain and snow
It measures the temperature of the ground
check.why: Radar sends out radio waves; precipitation bounces them back, showing where it is.

check.q: Why do forecasters release weather balloons?
choices: To mark where storms will hit
To measure conditions high above the ground
To scare birds away from airports
check.why: Balloons carry instruments miles up, reporting temperature, wind and moisture aloft.

check.q: Why is a forecast for seven days from now less certain than one for tomorrow?
choices: Computers turn off after one day
Small errors in the air's motion grow over time
Satellites only look one day ahead
check.why: Tiny differences in the starting data grow bigger each day the model runs forward.

review.q: Which of these is a climate fact about Illinois?
choices: Winters are usually cold and summers hot
review.why: Climate describes the usual pattern over many years, not one day's weather.

review.q: Which tool measures how much rain fell?
review.why: A rain gauge is a marked, straight-sided tube that catches rain so its depth can be read.

review.q: The flag points north, so the wind is coming from the
review.why: A flag points the way the wind is going. Wind is named for where it comes from, the south.

review.q: What does a tornado watch mean?
choices: Conditions are right for tornadoes; be ready
Tornadoes are over for the day
You should drive to look for one
review.why: A watch means ingredients are present. A warning means a tornado is happening now.

review.q: Why does Seattle, near the ocean, have milder winters than a city far inland?
choices: Ocean water heats and cools slowly
It is closer to the equator
It sits in a rain shadow
review.why: Big bodies of water change temperature slowly, keeping nearby air from getting as cold.

review.q: Which cloud type is thin, high and made of ice crystals?
review.why: Cirrus clouds are the high, wispy curls of ice crystals.

review.q: What did Luke Howard contribute to weather science in 1803?
choices: The names we still use for clouds
review.why: Howard named cloud types cumulus, stratus and cirrus, names still used today.

review.q: A town builds a levee. What is a possible trade-off?
choices: More water may be pushed toward the next town
review.why: Holding water back in one place can send more of it downstream, so designs have costs.

chapters.title: Earth's Changing Surface
chapters.bigQuestion: How can rocks, layers, rivers and ice tell us how Earth's surface has changed and is changing still?

story.title: Why Illinois Is So Flat
story.kicker: The corn goes on forever because a wall of ice once went on forever too.
paragraphs: Drive south out of Chicago on Interstate 57. For hours the land is flat as a tabletop. Corn and soybeans stretch to the edge of the sky. A visitor from Colorado asks, 'Where are the hills?' The answer is buried under her feet, in the dirt. It begins about 20,000 years ago.

Back then, northern Illinois was under ice. Not a frozen pond. A sheet of ice thousands of feet thick, in places close to a mile. It had crept down from Canada over thousands of years. It was so heavy it pressed the ground down. Nothing lived on top of it.

Ice that thick does not sit still. It flows, slowly, like very thick pancake batter. As it flowed, it scraped the ground beneath it. It shaved off hilltops. It picked up rocks, sand and clay and carried them along, frozen inside. Some rocks came all the way from Canada.

Then the climate warmed. The ice melted back, north, a little each year. Everything it had been carrying dropped out. Sand, clay, gravel and boulders spread across the land in a thick blanket. Where the ice paused, it left long, low ridges. Melting water washed the rest smooth.

So when you see flat Illinois, you are seeing the floor the ice left behind. Dig a well and you hit that blanket of rock bits. It can be hundreds of feet deep. The hills are still there, underneath. This chapter is about water, ice, wind and time. They keep changing the ground we stand on.
story.think: The story says rocks from Canada are found in Illinois fields. What evidence would convince you that ice, not a river, carried them here?

lessons.title: Layers Like Pages
lessons.mainIdea: Rock forms in layers, with the oldest at the bottom, so a cliff is a stack of Earth's history.
reading: Look at a road cut where a highway slices through a hill. You will often see stripes. Each stripe is a *layer* of rock. Layers form when mud, sand or tiny shells settle at the bottom of water and slowly harden. New layers pile on top of old ones.

That gives us a rule. In an undisturbed stack, the bottom layer is the *oldest*. The top layer is the youngest. It is like a pile of newspapers on a porch. The paper on the bottom was delivered first. Geologists, scientists who study rock, read a cliff from the bottom up.

Layers also tell what a place used to be. Sandstone made of tiny grains means an old beach or desert. Limestone full of shell pieces means a shallow warm sea. Much of Illinois sits on limestone. Long ago, this land was under a sea.

words.d: one flat band of rock that formed on top of an older band
formed first, the longest time ago
a scientist who studies rocks and how Earth changes

look.title: The Cliff by the River
look.text: A cliff shows four layers. From the bottom: gray limestone with shell pieces, then tan sandstone, then a thin black band of coal, then brown clay on top. A student says the coal formed first because it is black and 'looks old.' Another says the limestone formed first.
look.prompt: Who is right, and what does the order of the layers say about how this place changed over time?

check.q: In a stack of rock layers that has not been disturbed, where is the oldest layer?
check.why: New layers form on top of old ones, so the bottom layer formed first.

check.q: A layer of limestone is full of shell pieces. What was this place long ago?
check.why: Shells come from sea animals, so shell-filled limestone means an old sea floor.

check.q: How do most rock layers form?
choices: Mud and sand settle in water and harden
check.why: Layers build up as sediment settles at the bottom of water and slowly turns to rock.

lessons.title: Fossils in the Rock
lessons.mainIdea: Fossils are traces of living things preserved in rock, and they show that Illinois was once a warm swamp.
reading: A *fossil* is the remains or mark of a living thing kept in rock. It might be a bone, a shell, a leaf print or a footprint. Fossils form when a dead plant or animal is buried fast in mud. It has to be buried before it rots. Over a very long time, the mud becomes rock. The shape stays.

Near Braidwood, southwest of Chicago, is Mazon Creek. About 300 million years ago it was a steamy swamp by the sea. Ferns as tall as trees grew there. Their buried remains became the coal Illinois still mines. Inside hard lumps of rock, collectors find leaves, insects and strange sea creatures.

The strangest is the Tully monster, found by a collector named Francis Tully in the 1950s. It had a long snout, eyes on stalks and a soft body. Nothing like it lives today. It is the Illinois state fossil. Fossils like this are evidence that life, and the land, has changed enormously.

words.d: the remains or mark of a plant or animal preserved in rock
warm, wet, muddy land where plants grow thick

look.title: A Fern in the Coal
look.text: A coal miner in southern Illinois cracks open a chunk of dark rock. Inside is the perfect print of a fern leaf. Coal is burned to make electricity. It sits hundreds of feet below cornfields. Yet ferns need sun, warmth and wet ground. Today the winters here freeze solid.
look.prompt: What does the fern print tell you about what this land was like when the coal formed?

check.q: Which of these could become a fossil?
choices: A leaf buried quickly in mud
A leaf left on a sunny sidewalk
check.why: Fossils form when living things are buried fast in mud that later becomes rock.

check.q: What do the Mazon Creek fossils show about Illinois 300 million years ago?
choices: It was a tall mountain range
It was a warm swamp near the sea
check.why: Fossil ferns, insects and sea creatures show a warm, wet swamp by the sea.

check.q: Why is the Tully monster important evidence?
choices: It is still alive in Illinois rivers
It was the biggest animal ever
It proves Illinois never had oceans
It shows that living things have changed a great deal over time
check.why: An animal unlike anything alive today shows life has changed enormously since then.

lessons.title: The Canyon's Story
lessons.mainIdea: The Grand Canyon's mile-deep walls show layer after layer that a river slowly cut through.
reading: In 1869, John Wesley Powell led nine men in wooden boats down the Colorado River. Nobody had mapped its canyons. Powell had lost an arm in the Civil War. He rode in a chair strapped to a boat and wrote notes about the rock walls rising around him.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is about 277 miles long and more than a mile deep. Its walls are a stack of layers, oldest at the bottom. Powell saw that the river had cut down through all of them. Sand carried by fast water works like sandpaper on rock.

The lesson is *time*. A river cannot carve a mile of rock in a year, or a thousand years. It takes millions. The canyon is evidence that slow, steady change, given enough time, can do enormous work. Geologists call this 'deep time.'

words.d: a deep, narrow valley with steep rock walls, usually cut by a river
how long something takes; Earth's surface changes over enormous spans of it

look.title: Powell Enters the Unknown
look.text: In August 1869, before pushing off into the deepest part of the canyon, Powell wrote in his journal that the party was ready to start down what he called the great unknown. Their boats were battered, their food was nearly gone, and the walls rose higher than any they had seen.
look.cite: John Wesley Powell, river expedition journal, 1869
look.prompt: Powell wrote his notes on the river instead of waiting until he got home. Why does that matter for science?

check.q: What carved the Grand Canyon?
choices: Wind blew the rock away in a few years
The Colorado River cut down through rock over millions of years
check.why: The river, carrying sand, slowly wore down through the layers over an enormous span of time.

check.q: Where are the oldest rocks in the Grand Canyon?
choices: At the bottom by the river
check.why: Layers stack with the oldest at the bottom, so the deepest rock is the oldest.

check.q: What does the canyon show about slow changes?
choices: Only fast changes shape the land
Given enough time, slow changes can do enormous work
check.why: A river wears rock a little at a time, but over millions of years it cut a mile deep.

lessons.title: Weathering Breaks Rock
lessons.mainIdea: Weathering is the breaking of rock into smaller pieces by water, ice, plants and temperature changes.
reading: Rock seems forever. It is not. *Weathering* is anything that breaks rock into smaller bits without moving it away. The biggest tool in Illinois is ice. Water seeps into a crack. At night it freezes. Ice takes up more room than water, so it pushes the crack wider.

Do it a hundred times and the rock splits. That is why Chicago streets grow potholes every spring. Water gets under the pavement, freezes, thaws and freezes again. Tree roots do the same thing more slowly. A root grows into a crack and pushes as it thickens.

Water also weathers rock by dissolving it. Rain is very slightly acidic. Limestone slowly melts away in it. Over ages this hollows out caves. Even sunlight helps. Rock heats and expands by day, cools and shrinks by night. Little by little, the surface crumbles.

words.d: the breaking of rock into smaller pieces by ice, water, plants or heat
to mix into water and disappear, the way sugar does

look.title: The Pothole Season
look.text: In November, a crack in the street is thin as a pencil line. Rain fills it. On cold nights the water freezes. On warm days it melts and more water gets in. By March, the crack is a hole 2 feet wide. The city fills it. Next year, a new hole opens beside it.
look.prompt: Why do potholes form mostly in winter and early spring, and not in July?

check.q: How does freezing water break rock?
choices: Ice takes up more room than water and pushes cracks wider
check.why: Water expands when it freezes, so ice in a crack wedges it open a bit more each time.

check.q: Which of these is an example of weathering?
choices: Wind piling sand into a dune
Mud settling at the bottom of a lake
A tree root splitting a boulder
check.why: Weathering breaks rock in place. The root splits the rock without moving it.

check.q: Why do caves often form in limestone?
choices: Slightly acidic water slowly dissolves limestone
Limestone is soft enough to dig
check.why: Rain is a little acidic, and over ages it dissolves limestone, hollowing out caves.

lessons.title: Erosion Carries It Away
lessons.mainIdea: Erosion is the moving of rock pieces and soil by water, ice, wind or gravity.
reading: Weathering breaks rock. *Erosion* moves the pieces somewhere else. Water is the champion mover. A creek after a storm runs brown because it is full of soil. Rivers carry sand and mud toward the sea. The faster the water, the bigger the pieces it can carry.

Wind erodes too, mostly in dry places. It lifts sand and dust and drops it far away. Dust from farm fields once blew all the way from Kansas to the East Coast in the 1930s. *Gravity* pulls loose rock downhill in landslides. Ice, as you read, drags whole boulders.

Plants slow erosion. Roots hold soil in place. Leaves soften the blow of rain. When a hillside is cleared, the next storm can wash it bare. Farmers in Illinois plant cover crops and leave old stalks on the field to keep the soil from blowing or washing away.

words.d: the carrying away of rock pieces and soil by water, wind, ice or gravity
the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth
a sudden slide of rock and soil down a slope

look.title: Two Hills in a Storm
look.text: Two hills sit side by side. One is covered with prairie grass and deep roots. The other was bulldozed bare last week. A hard rain falls for an hour. The creek below the grassy hill runs nearly clear. The creek below the bare hill runs thick and brown, and a gully has opened in the slope.
look.prompt: Where did the brown color come from, and what did the grass do that the bare hill could not?

check.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
choices: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves the pieces
Weathering moves rock; erosion breaks it
check.why: Weathering breaks rock in place. Erosion carries the broken bits away.

check.q: Why does a creek run brown after a heavy rain?
choices: It is carrying soil washed from the land
check.why: Fast rainwater picks up soil and carries it, coloring the creek brown.

check.q: How do plant roots reduce erosion?
choices: They hold soil in place against water and wind
check.why: Roots grip soil so water and wind cannot carry it off as easily.

lessons.title: Deposition Builds New Land
lessons.mainIdea: When moving water, wind or ice slows down, it drops what it carries, and that builds new land.
reading: Everything that erodes has to land somewhere. *Deposition* is the dropping of rock bits and soil when water, wind or ice slows down. Fast water carries pebbles. Slow water can only carry the finest mud. So as a river slows, it drops the heavy stuff first.

Where a river meets the sea, it slows almost to a stop. It drops its load in a fan of mud called a *delta*. The Mississippi River has built a huge delta in Louisiana out of soil from Illinois, Iowa and a dozen other states. New land grows there year by year.

You can see deposition on a small scale. After a flood, a thin layer of mud coats the grass. Sandbars appear on the inside of a river bend, where the water is slowest. Wind drops sand into dunes at the Indiana Dunes, just around the lake from Chicago.

words.d: the dropping of rock pieces and soil when water, wind or ice slows down
a fan of new land built where a river drops its mud at the sea or a lake
a ridge of sand dropped by slow water in a river or along a shore

look.title: The Jar of Muddy Water
look.text: A student fills a jar with creek water, gravel, sand and mud, and shakes it hard. Everything swirls together. She sets it down. In seconds the gravel is on the bottom. In a minute the sand has settled on top of it. Hours later, the water is finally clear, with a fine mud layer on top.
look.prompt: Why did the gravel settle first? What does this tell you about where a slowing river drops pebbles versus mud?

check.q: When does a river drop the rock and soil it is carrying?
check.why: Slow water cannot hold heavy pieces, so a slowing river deposits its load.

check.q: What is a delta?
choices: A deep canyon cut by a river
A crack made by freezing water
A hill left by a glacier
New land built where a river drops mud at the sea
check.why: A delta is the fan of deposited mud and sand where a river slows at the sea.

check.q: A river slows down. Which will it drop first?
check.why: Heavy pebbles settle first; fine mud stays in the water longest.

lessons.title: Fast Changes and Slow Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Some changes to Earth's surface happen in minutes, others take millions of years, and both leave evidence.
reading: A landslide can move a hillside in a minute. A volcano can bury a town in a day. On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington exploded. The top 1,300 feet of the mountain was gone in minutes. Those are *rapid* changes. They are dramatic but rare.

Most change is slow. Niagara Falls has been wearing back its cliff for thousands of years, now at about a foot a year. The Grand Canyon took millions. In the 1780s, a Scottish farmer and doctor named James Hutton looked at rock layers and saw slow change everywhere.

Hutton argued that the same processes we see today made the land. Rain, rivers, ice and waves did the work, over unimaginable time. He wrote that he could find no sign of a beginning. He could find no sign of an end. The present is the key to the past. That idea is the heart of geology.

words.d: very fast; happening in minutes, hours or days
a series of actions that keeps happening, like rain wearing away rock

look.title: Hutton's Endless Earth
look.text: Hutton ended his 1788 report on the Earth by saying that after all his study of the rocks, he could find no trace of a beginning and no sign of an end. The forces shaping the land, he argued, had always been at work and were still at work.
look.cite: James Hutton, Theory of the Earth, 1788
look.prompt: What evidence in a road cut or riverbank could support Hutton's idea that the same slow processes are still going on today?

check.q: Which is an example of a rapid change to Earth's surface?
check.why: A volcanic eruption changes the land in minutes or hours. The others take ages.

check.q: What was James Hutton's big idea?
choices: Earth was made in a single day
Volcanoes made all the rock layers
The slow processes we see today shaped the land over enormous time
check.why: Hutton saw that everyday processes like rain and rivers, given time, explain the rocks.

check.q: Niagara Falls wears back about a foot a year. In 100 years, roughly how far will it move?
check.why: One foot a year for 100 years is about 100 feet. Slow rates add up.

lessons.title: Rivers of Ice
lessons.mainIdea: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that flows slowly and scrapes, carries and drops rock as it goes.
reading: A *glacier* is ice so thick that it moves. Snow piles up faster than it melts, year after year. The weight squeezes the bottom into ice. Then the whole mass creeps downhill or spreads out, a few feet a year. It looks frozen still. Over decades, it flows.

Glaciers are bulldozers. The bottom of the ice is studded with rocks. As the ice slides, those rocks scratch and grind the ground beneath. They leave long scratches on bedrock that point the way the ice moved. The ice plucks boulders loose and carries them frozen inside.

During the last *ice age*, sheets of ice covered Canada and spread south. Ice reached almost 90 percent of Illinois at one time or another. It went farther south here than anywhere else in North America, close to Carbondale. The ice finally melted out of Illinois roughly 14,000 years ago.

words.d: a huge mass of ice that moves slowly over land
a long cold time when glaciers covered much more of Earth than they do now
the solid rock under the soil and loose material

look.title: Scratches on the Rock
look.text: In a quarry near Chicago, workers clear away 30 feet of clay and gravel and reach solid limestone. Its surface is polished smooth. Long parallel scratches run across it, all pointing the same direction, from northeast to southwest. A boulder of pink granite sits nearby. There is no granite in Illinois.
look.prompt: What made the scratches, why do they all point the same way, and how did the granite get there?

check.q: What makes a glacier move?
choices: Its own huge weight makes the ice slowly flow
check.why: Ice thick enough becomes heavy enough to creep and flow under its own weight.

check.q: Scratches on bedrock all run northeast to southwest. What do they show?
choices: Where a river used to be
check.why: Rocks frozen in the bottom of moving ice scratch the ground in the direction of flow.

check.q: About when did the last glaciers melt out of Illinois?
check.why: The last ice sheet melted back out of Illinois roughly 14,000 years ago.

lessons.title: What the Ice Left Behind
lessons.mainIdea: Melting glaciers dropped a thick blanket of rock, sand and clay that made Illinois flat and its soil rich.
reading: When a glacier melts, it drops everything it carried. That jumbled mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders is called *till*. Till covers most of Illinois, in places more than 100 feet deep. It buried the old hills and valleys. That is the flat land you see.

Sometimes the ice edge stood still for a while. Then till piled up in a long ridge called a *moraine*. Northeast Illinois has many of them. They are low hills curving around the south end of Lake Michigan. The lake itself sits in a basin the ice scooped out. Meltwater filled it.

The ice gave Illinois something else: some of the best farm soil on Earth. Wind picked up fine dust from the melting glacier's outwash and spread it across the state. Ground-up rock is full of minerals plants need. Prairie grass grew, died and rotted into it for thousands of years.

words.d: the jumbled mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders a glacier drops when it melts
a long ridge of till piled up at the edge of a glacier

look.title: How High Is High?
look.cite: USGS and standard reference values, rounded
look.prompt: Charles Mound, in the corner of Illinois the ice never reached, is the state's highest point. Why might the highest ground be in the one unglaciated corner?

check.q: What is till?
choices: A jumbled mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders left by ice
Sand dropped by a slow river
check.why: Till is the unsorted material a glacier drops when it melts.

check.q: Why is most of Illinois flat?
choices: Rivers wore all the hills away
Glaciers buried the old hills under thick till
check.why: Melting ice dropped a blanket of till up to hundreds of feet deep over the old land.

check.q: What is a moraine?
choices: A ridge of till piled at a glacier's edge
check.why: Where the ice edge paused, till built up into a long, low ridge called a moraine.

lessons.title: Maps of Quakes and Volcanoes
lessons.mainIdea: Earthquakes and volcanoes are not scattered randomly; they line up in belts around Earth.
reading: Put every *earthquake* of the last fifty years on a world map. They do not spread out evenly. They cluster in long, narrow belts. A giant belt circles the Pacific Ocean, through Japan, Alaska, California and Chile. Volcanoes line up in the same belt. It is called the Ring of Fire.

The pattern is evidence. Earth's outer shell is broken into huge slabs called *plates*. They creep about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where they push, pull or grind against each other, rock breaks and shakes. Melted rock rises. That is why the belts exist.

Illinois is far from any plate edge, but not safe from shaking. In the winter of 1811 and 1812, huge earthquakes near New Madrid, Missouri, cracked the ground in southern Illinois. Reports say the Mississippi River briefly ran backward. Small quakes still rattle that area.

words.d: a shaking of the ground caused by rock suddenly breaking or slipping deep in Earth
one of the huge slabs that make up Earth's outer shell
an opening where melted rock, ash and gas come up from inside Earth

look.title: Some of the Biggest Earthquakes
look.prompt: Four of these five happened on the Ring of Fire. Which one did not, and what does that tell you about the middle of a plate?

check.q: Where do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
choices: Spread evenly over the whole Earth
check.why: Maps show quakes and volcanoes clustered in belts along plate edges, like the Ring of Fire.

check.q: About how fast do Earth's plates move?
choices: As fast as a walking person
About as fast as fingernails grow
They do not move at all
check.why: Plates creep a few centimeters a year, roughly the speed fingernails grow.

check.q: What happened near New Madrid in 1811 and 1812?
choices: Huge earthquakes shook the middle of the country
The Ring of Fire moved to Missouri
check.why: Powerful earthquakes struck the New Madrid area, far from any plate edge.

lessons.title: Designing for Shaking and Flooding
lessons.mainIdea: People cannot stop earthquakes or floods, but maps and smart design can keep more people safe.
reading: The first tool is a map. If earthquakes cluster in belts, builders know where to be careful. In California, buildings are made to sway instead of snap. Steel frames bend. Heavy water tanks are strapped down. In Japan, some towers sit on rubber pads that soak up shaking.

Rivers have patterns too. A *floodplain* is the flat land beside a river that floods every so often. Maps show which land floods often. Some towns keep floodplains as parks and farms, not houses. Others build levees or raise homes on posts.

Every choice is a *trade-off*. Stronger buildings cost more. Leaving a floodplain empty means less land for homes. Engineers and towns weigh the danger, how often it comes, and what they can afford. Knowing the pattern is what makes the choice possible.

words.d: the flat land beside a river that gets covered with water when the river floods
something you give up to get something else

look.title: The Empty Field by the River
look.text: A town on the Illinois River has an empty field between the water and Main Street. Records show it flooded in 1943, 1979, 1993 and 2013. A builder wants to put 40 houses there. A neighbor wants a soccer park. The mayor wants tax money from the houses.
look.prompt: Using the flood record as evidence, what would you advise the town to do, and what is the trade-off of your choice?

check.q: Why are some buildings in earthquake country designed to sway?
choices: A building that bends is less likely to snap and fall
check.why: Frames that flex absorb shaking instead of breaking.

check.q: What is a floodplain?
choices: A wall built to stop floods
A deep part of a river
Flat land beside a river that floods now and then
check.why: The floodplain is the low, flat land a river spills onto when it rises.

check.q: Why do maps of past earthquakes and floods help engineers?
choices: They show where danger is most likely, so design can match it
They tell exactly when the next one will hit
check.why: Patterns in the past show where to expect trouble, so builders can plan for it.

review.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the layer on top is
review.why: New layers form on top of old ones, so the top is the most recent.

review.q: Which process moves broken rock and soil from one place to another?
review.why: Erosion is the carrying away of rock bits by water, wind, ice or gravity.

review.q: A river drops sand and mud where it meets the sea, building a delta. This is an example of
review.why: Deposition is the dropping of carried material when water slows down.

review.q: Why does Illinois have so few hills?
choices: Melting glaciers buried the old land under thick till
Rivers carried them to the sea
review.why: Glaciers dropped a thick blanket of till that covered the old hills and valleys.

review.q: Which is the slowest change on this list?
review.why: Carving a canyon takes millions of years. The others happen in minutes, hours or days.

review.q: What pattern do earthquakes and volcanoes show on a world map?
choices: They line up in belts along plate edges
They only happen near the equator
review.why: Quakes and volcanoes cluster where plates meet, such as the Ring of Fire.

review.q: A fossil fern is found in Illinois coal. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Ferns can grow in coal today
Illinois was once warm and swampy
review.why: Ferns need warmth and wet ground, so the land was a swamp when the coal formed.

review.q: Freezing water splits a rock. Which process is this?
review.why: Weathering breaks rock in place. Ice wedging is one kind of weathering.

chapters.title: Earth in Space
chapters.bigQuestion: What patterns in the sky can we see and measure, and what do they tell us about Earth's place in space?

story.title: The Shadow Stick on the Blacktop
story.kicker: A broom handle, a piece of chalk and one school day are enough to catch the Earth turning.
paragraphs: At 8:30 in the morning, Ms. Ortiz's class carried a bucket of sand and a broom handle out to the blacktop. They stood the handle straight up in the bucket. The sun was low in the east. The shadow of the stick stretched long across the pavement, pointing west. Devon traced its tip in chalk and wrote the time.

Every hour a different student ran out to mark it. By 10:30 the shadow had swung toward the northwest and gotten shorter. At 12:30 it was the shortest of the day. It pointed straight north, at the flagpole. By 2:30 it was growing again, sliding toward the northeast. The chalk marks made a curve.

Back inside, Devon had a question. 'The stick never moved. The bucket never moved. So what moved?' Half the class said the sun moved across the sky. The other half remembered something about the Earth spinning. Ms. Ortiz did not answer. She asked them to think about a merry-go-round.

When you spin on a merry-go-round, the playground seems to sweep past you. The slide, the fence, the trees all go by. But they are standing still. You are the one turning. Devon got it first. 'We are on the merry-go-round. The sun is the tree.' The sun only seems to travel. Earth is turning under it.

The next week they did it again, and the curve had shifted a little. The noon shadow was a bit shorter. The days were getting longer. Something else was changing, more slowly than the daily spin. This chapter follows those chalk marks: the day, the year, the moon and the stars, all from a stick in a bucket.
story.think: The shortest shadow of the day pointed north, toward the flagpole. Where in the sky was the sun at that moment?

lessons.title: Our Star, the Sun
lessons.mainIdea: The sun is a star like the ones at night; it looks huge and bright only because it is so much closer.
reading: The sun is a *star*. That may sound odd, because it does not look like the tiny sparks in the night sky. But it is the same kind of thing. It is a giant ball of hot gas that makes its own light. The night stars are suns too, unimaginably far away.

The sun is close, as stars go. It is about 93 million miles from Earth. Light is the fastest thing there is, and it still takes about 8 minutes to make the trip. When you feel sunlight on your face, it left the sun 8 minutes ago.

The sun is also enormous. About 109 Earths could line up across its middle. It looks small because it is far away, the way a jet looks like a speck when it is miles up. Never look straight at the sun. Its light is strong enough to hurt your eyes for good.

words.d: a giant ball of hot gas in space that makes its own light and heat
how far apart two things are

look.title: The Flashlight Down the Hall
look.text: Two identical flashlights are turned on in a dark hallway. One is held 3 feet from you. The other is carried all the way to the far end, 100 feet away. The near one looks big and bright and makes you squint. The far one is a small dot. Both bulbs are putting out the same light.
look.prompt: How is this like the sun and the night stars? What would you need to know to tell whether a dim star is actually small, or just far away?

check.q: What is the sun?
choices: A giant ball of burning wood
A star that makes its own light
check.why: The sun is a star: a huge ball of hot gas that produces its own light and heat.

check.q: Why does the sun look so much bigger and brighter than other stars?
choices: It is the biggest star in the universe
It is the only star that gives off light
It is made of different stuff
It is much closer to Earth
check.why: The sun is a normal-sized star, but it is millions of times closer than any other star.

check.q: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. What does that tell you?
choices: The sun is very far away even though light is very fast
The sun turns off every 8 minutes
check.why: Light is the fastest thing known, so an 8-minute trip means an enormous distance.

lessons.title: Why Stars Look Different
lessons.mainIdea: Stars look brighter or dimmer mostly because of how far away they are, and their distances are enormous.
reading: Look up on a clear night. Some stars are bright. Some you can barely see. Two things decide that. One is how much light the star really gives off. The other is *distance*. A bright star far away can look dimmer than a weak star nearby.

Star distances are so big that miles stop being useful. Astronomers use the *light-year*, the distance light travels in one year. That is about 6 trillion miles. The nearest star after the sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4 light-years away. Its light left it four years ago.

Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is about 8.6 light-years away. Some stars you can see are hundreds of light-years off. Their light left them before your grandparents were born. Looking at stars is looking back in time.

words.d: the distance light travels in one year, about 6 trillion miles
a scientist who studies stars, planets and space

look.title: How Far Is Far?
look.prompt: Sirius looks brighter than Proxima Centauri even though it is twice as far away. What must be true about Sirius?

check.q: What is a light-year?
choices: The time it takes Earth to circle the sun
One year on a distant planet
The distance light travels in one year
check.why: A light-year measures distance, not time: how far light goes in a year.

check.q: Two stars give off the same amount of light. One is 10 light-years away and one is 100. Which looks brighter?
check.why: The closer star looks brighter, just like the near flashlight in the hall.

check.q: You see a star 100 light-years away. When did the light you see leave it?
check.why: Light took 100 years to cross 100 light-years, so you are seeing the star as it was 100 years ago.

lessons.title: Patterns in the Night Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Stars form patterns that stay the same night after night, so people have used them as a map.
reading: Stars do not move around compared to each other. The same groups appear in the same shapes year after year. People long ago connected them into pictures and gave them names. Those groups are *constellations*. The Big Dipper, with its seven bright stars, is one part of a larger one.

The Big Dipper is a good starting point in Illinois. It can be seen on any clear night of the year. Follow the two stars at the end of its bowl and you reach Polaris, the North Star. Polaris sits almost straight above Earth's North Pole, so it always marks north.

Sailors and travelers steered by Polaris for centuries. Before compasses, before maps, the stars were the map. Once you learn a few constellations, the night sky stops being random dots. It becomes a place with landmarks, and you can find your way in it.

words.d: a group of stars that people see as a pattern or picture
the North Star; it sits almost above Earth's North Pole and always marks north

look.title: Lost in the Dark
look.text: A camper in downstate Illinois walks away from the tent at night and loses the trail. There is no phone signal. The sky is clear. She remembers that the tent is north of the road. She finds the Big Dipper and follows the two stars at the end of its bowl to a medium-bright star that does not seem to move.
look.prompt: How can she use that star to walk back toward the road, and why does it work no matter what time of night it is?

check.q: What is a constellation?
choices: A star that moves across the sky
A group of stars seen as a pattern
check.why: Constellations are star groups that people connect into shapes and name.

check.q: Why does Polaris always show north?
choices: It sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole
It rises in the north every evening
check.why: Because it lies above the pole Earth spins around, it barely moves as Earth turns.

check.q: Why are the constellations the same shape every year?
choices: Stars are so far away that their motion is too small to notice
The sky is a painted dome
check.why: Stars do move, but they are so distant that the patterns look fixed for thousands of years.

lessons.title: Earth Spins
lessons.mainIdea: Earth rotates once every 24 hours, and that spin is what makes day and night.
reading: Earth is a ball spinning in space. It turns all the way around once every 24 hours. That spin is called *rotation*. Earth rotates around an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, its *axis*. You cannot feel the spin because everything around you spins with you.

Half of Earth always faces the sun. That half has day. The other half faces away, into dark space. That half has night. As Earth turns, your town swings from the dark side into the lit side. That is sunrise. Later it swings back into the dark. That is sunset.

It is tempting to say the sun goes around Earth. It looks that way. But if the sun moved and Earth sat still, the stars would have to circle us every day too, and so would the moon, all at the same speed. One spinning Earth explains everything at once. That is why scientists trust it.

words.d: spinning around a center line, the way a top spins
the imaginary line through the North and South Poles that Earth spins around

look.title: The Lamp and the Orange
look.text: In a dark room, a lamp stands for the sun. A student holds an orange with a pin stuck in it for Chicago. She turns the orange slowly. The pin comes into the light: morning. It faces the lamp straight on: noon. It slides into shadow: evening. It spends a while in the dark, then comes back into the light.
look.prompt: In this model, what does one full turn of the orange stand for? What would you have to change to make Chicago's day longer?

check.q: What causes day and night?
choices: The sun turning on and off
check.why: As Earth rotates, each place turns into the sunlight and then away from it.

check.q: How long does one full rotation of Earth take?
check.why: One spin takes about 24 hours, which is one day.

check.q: Why can't you feel Earth spinning?
choices: Earth spins too slowly to matter
The spin only happens at night
Everything around you is spinning along with you
check.why: The ground, the air and you all move together, so nothing seems to move.

lessons.title: The Sun's Daily Path
lessons.mainIdea: Because Earth spins, the sun appears to rise in the east, climb high toward the south, and set in the west.
reading: Earth spins toward the east. So the sun seems to come up in the east. It climbs higher through the morning. In Illinois, it is never straight overhead. At *noon* it is highest, and it stands in the southern half of the sky. Then it sinks and sets in the west.

That path is why south-facing windows get the most sun. It is why a sidewalk on the north side of a building stays icy longest. It is why the noon shadow of a stick points north. The sun is to the south, so the shadow falls the other way.

The path changes a little with the seasons. In summer the sun rises in the northeast and climbs very high. In winter it rises in the southeast and stays low. But east to west, low to high to low, is the same every single day. It is one of the most reliable patterns on Earth.

words.d: the middle of the day, when the sun is highest in the sky
the line where the sky seems to meet the ground

look.title: The Icy Sidewalk
look.text: A week after a snowstorm, the sidewalk on the south side of the school is dry. The sidewalk on the north side, right against the building, is still a sheet of ice. Both got the same snow. The custodian salted both. The building is three stories tall.
look.prompt: Why did the south side melt first? Where is the sun during the school day, and what does the building do to the north side?

check.q: Where does the sun appear to rise?
check.why: Earth spins toward the east, so the sun first appears on the eastern horizon.

check.q: At noon in Illinois, where is the sun?
check.why: From Illinois the noon sun is high but always in the southern half of the sky.

check.q: A stick's shadow at noon points north. What does that tell you about the sun?
choices: The sun is to the south
The sun is to the north
check.why: Shadows fall away from the light, so a north-pointing shadow means the sun is in the south.

lessons.title: Shadows Through the Day
lessons.mainIdea: A shadow's length and direction change through the day in a pattern that tracks the sun's path.
reading: A *shadow* is the dark spot where something blocks the light. Your shadow stretches away from the sun. When the sun is low, near the horizon, shadows are long. When the sun is high, shadows are short. That is the whole rule, and it makes a shadow a clock.

In the morning the sun is low in the east. Shadows are long and point west. By noon the sun is high in the south. Shadows are short and point north. In the afternoon the sun sinks toward the west. Shadows grow long again, pointing east.

People used this for thousands of years. A *sundial* is just a stick and a set of marks. Record the shadow every hour for one day. Then the marks tell time on any sunny day. You can also check the pattern. It repeats, day after day, with tiny changes through the year.

words.d: the dark area behind something that blocks light
a clock made from a stick and marks; the stick's shadow points to the time

look.title: The Shadow Stick Log
look.unit: inches, shadow length of a 24-inch stick
look.cite: a class record on a spring day in Illinois, rounded
look.prompt: When was the shadow shortest? Why is the 1 p.m. shadow still almost as long as the stick, even at the sun's highest point?

check.q: When are shadows shortest?
choices: When the sun is low in the sky
When the sun is highest in the sky
check.why: A high sun makes light come down steeply, so the shadow is short.

check.q: In the morning, a stick's shadow points west. Where is the sun?
check.why: Shadows point away from the light, so a west-pointing shadow means the sun is in the east.

check.q: How can a shadow work like a clock?
choices: The shadow's direction and length change in a repeating daily pattern
Shadows always point at the time
Shadows only appear at certain times
check.why: Because the sun's path repeats each day, the shadow at each hour lands in the same place.

sections.title: The Year, the Moon and Gravity

lessons.title: Why We Have Seasons
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's tilt, not its distance from the sun, causes the seasons by changing how directly sunlight hits us.
reading: Earth travels around the sun once a year. That trip is its *orbit*. Earth's axis is tilted, about 23.5 degrees, and the tilt always points the same way in space. For part of the year the northern half leans toward the sun. For the other part it leans away.

When Illinois leans toward the sun, the sun climbs high and days are long. Sunlight hits the ground more directly and heats it more. That is summer. Chicago gets about 15 hours of daylight in late June. When Illinois leans away, the sun stays low and days are short, about 9 hours in late December. That is winter.

Many people think summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun. It is not true. Earth is actually a little closer to the sun in January. The *tilt* is what matters. That is also why Australia has summer while Illinois has winter. The southern half is leaning toward the sun then.

words.d: the path one object takes around another, like Earth around the sun
a lean to one side; Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees
hitting straight on rather than at a slant

look.title: The Flashlight on the Table
look.text: Shine a flashlight straight down on a table. It makes a small, bright circle. Now tilt the flashlight so the beam hits at a slant. The same light spreads into a long, dim oval. The flashlight did not change. The bulb is the same distance away. Only the angle changed.
look.prompt: Which patch of table would warm up more? How does this explain why winter sunlight, low and slanting, feels weak?

check.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
choices: Earth's distance from the sun changing
The sun getting hotter and cooler
The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the sun
check.why: The tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each half of Earth through the year.

check.q: When it is summer in Illinois, what season is it in Australia?
check.why: The southern half leans away from the sun when the northern half leans toward it.

check.q: Earth is slightly closer to the sun in January. Why isn't January warm in Illinois?
choices: The small distance change matters less than the tilt
The sun is dimmer in January
Earth is not really closer in January
check.why: The tilt makes January sunlight slanted and weak, which outweighs the small change in distance.

lessons.title: Stars of the Seasons
lessons.mainIdea: As Earth moves around the sun, the night side faces different directions, so different stars appear each season.
reading: Orion, the hunter with three stars in a row for a belt, rules the winter sky in Illinois. By July, it is gone. In its place, near the southern horizon, the curled tail of Scorpius appears. Then Orion comes back in December. The stars did not move. Earth did.

Night is the side of Earth facing away from the sun. As Earth goes around its orbit, that dark side points at a different part of space each season. In winter it points toward Orion. In summer it points the other way, toward Scorpius. Orion is still there in summer, but it is up during the day, lost in sunlight.

Some stars never leave. The Big Dipper and Polaris sit near the direction of Earth's axis. So they are visible all year from Illinois. Watching which constellations come and go is another pattern. This one takes a whole year to repeat.

words.d: a winter constellation with three bright stars in a row for a belt
changing with the seasons, repeating once a year

look.title: The Campfire Circle
look.text: Picture a campfire in the middle of a big field with a barn on one side and a pond on the other. You walk slowly in a circle around the fire, always facing away from it. When you are on the barn side, you see the pond. When you reach the pond side, you see the barn. You never see whatever is behind the fire.
look.prompt: What stands for the sun, Earth and the stars in this picture? Why can't you see 'summer stars' in winter?

check.q: Why can you see Orion in winter but not in summer?
choices: Orion moves to the other side of the sky
Earth's night side faces a different direction in each season
check.why: As Earth orbits, the dark side points at different stars; in summer Orion is up in daytime.

check.q: Which stars can be seen from Illinois all year?
check.why: Stars near the direction of Earth's axis, like Polaris, stay in view all year.

check.q: How long does the pattern of seasonal constellations take to repeat?
check.why: It follows Earth's orbit, which takes one year.

lessons.title: The Moon's Changing Face
lessons.mainIdea: The moon's phases repeat about every 29.5 days as we see different amounts of its sunlit half.
reading: The moon does not make its own light. It reflects sunlight. Half of the moon is always lit by the sun, just as half of Earth is. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see. The shapes we see are the *phases* of the moon.

The moon *orbits* Earth about once a month. When it is between Earth and the sun, its lit side faces away from us. We see nothing: a new moon. A week later we see half of it: first quarter. Two weeks in, the whole lit side faces us: full moon. Then it shrinks back.

The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days. In 1610, Galileo pointed one of the first telescopes at the moon. He saw mountains and craters, not a smooth glowing disk. He measured the mountains from their shadows. The moon was a world, with ground you could stand on.

words.d: the shape of the lit part of the moon that we see from Earth
a bowl-shaped hole made when a rock from space hits a surface
to bounce light back rather than make it

look.title: One Trip Around the Phases
look.prompt: If you saw a full moon on the 3rd of the month, about when would you expect the next full moon?

check.q: Where does the moon's light come from?
choices: The moon makes its own light
It reflects light from Earth's cities
check.why: The moon is rock. We see it because sunlight bounces off it.

check.q: About how long does it take the moon to go through all its phases?
check.why: The full cycle from new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.

check.q: What did Galileo discover about the moon in 1610?
check.why: Through his telescope Galileo saw shadows of mountains and craters on the moon's surface.

lessons.title: Down Means Toward the Center
lessons.mainIdea: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth's center, which is why 'down' points the same way everywhere on Earth.
reading: Drop a ball. It falls. Drop it in Chicago, in Australia, or at the South Pole. It falls toward the ground every time. *Gravity* is the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth. On a round planet, 'down' means toward the middle, wherever you stand.

That is why people in Australia do not fall off. Their 'down' points toward Earth's center too, just like yours. Gravity also holds the air close to Earth and keeps the moon circling us. It is the same pull, everywhere, all the time.

In July 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts landed on the moon. The moon's gravity is about one sixth as strong as Earth's, so they bounced in slow hops. But they did not float away. The moon pulled them toward its center, just as Earth pulls you. Gravity works on every world.

words.d: the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth or another large object
the middle point of something

check.why: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth's center, so 'down' means toward the middle.

check.q: Why don't people in Australia fall off Earth?
choices: Gravity pulls them toward Earth's center too
Australia is on top of Earth
check.why: Gravity points toward the center everywhere, so their down is toward the ground under them.

check.q: On the moon, astronauts bounced in slow hops. What does that show?
choices: The moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's but still pulls down
Earth's gravity reached them on the moon
check.why: The moon's pull is about one sixth of Earth's, so astronauts could hop high but still came down.

It is the only true star

review.why: The noon sun is high in the south, so the shadow is short and falls to the north.

It is hidden by the moon

It pushes things away from the ground
